answer: The Java heap is only one memory domain of the process. Overall process memory also includes thread stacks, native libraries, direct (off-heap) buffers, memory-mapped files, JIT/compiler code and other runtime structures, so a process or container can exceed its physical or configured memory limit even while recorded heap occupancy looks acceptable. That heap figure is also a sampled, collection-dependent observation: heap used before a collection is not a sufficient leak indicator, and a high allocation volume may reflect normal high-throughput churn rather than retained live data. Container limits are enforced against process/container accounting rather than the managed heap, so heap occupancy does not bound the process footprint. To attribute the growth, correlate JVM-side evidence (JFR/GC events, allocation and native-memory telemetry) with OS/container telemetry (memory limit, page faults) over the same load window: an allocation profile alone cannot establish a retained live-set or leak, and process metrics alone cannot show the application-level effect.
